title: Asking for help
description: Ask for instructions in a way that works for you.
introduction: Instructions can be confusing, especially when they come quickly. You can ask for a different explanation, written steps, or more time. You do not need to apologize for needing support.
scenario: You are in class with Ms. Morgan. She has just explained a new assignment aloud and moved on to helping another student. You caught some of the instructions, but you do not know which page to open or what to do first. You would like a clear first step and instructions you can check again.
opening: We’re starting the assignment now. What would help you get started?
question: What could you say or do to get instructions that work for you?

choices.text: Could you show me the first step? I did not catch which page to open.
choices.feedback: This names the part that is unclear and asks for one manageable step. You do not need to explain or apologize for needing clarity.

choices.text: Could you write the steps down so I can look at them as I work?
choices.feedback: Written steps give you something to return to. Asking for a different format is a valid accommodation.

choices.text: I need a moment to process that. Can you come back to me?
choices.feedback: You can ask for time before discussing the instructions again. You can use that time to decide what you need.

choices.text: I am not ready to ask yet.
choices.feedback: That is understandable. You can wait, use a communication card, or ask later. If you still need instructions, asking for a written first step is one option.

cards: Could you explain the first step again?
I need more time to process this.
takeaway: You deserve instructions you can understand.

title: Expressing your needs
description: Practice asking for a quieter space or a break.
introduction: Your comfort matters. You can explain what is difficult and ask for a change. You can also ask for a break without explaining everything about yourself.
scenario: You and Taylor are planning a class presentation at a table in a busy classroom. Other groups are talking nearby and chairs keep scraping across the floor. You are finding it hard to follow Taylor’s ideas or organize your own. A quieter table is available nearby, and you could also work together in writing or take a break.
opening: Let’s work on our project here. How would you like to begin?
question: How could you let Taylor know what would make working together easier?

choices.text: The noise is making it hard for me to focus. Can we move to the quieter table?
choices.feedback: This describes what is difficult and requests a specific change. Your sensory needs are valid.

choices.text: Could we write our ideas in a shared document instead of talking right now?
choices.feedback: This offers another communication method. You can ask for written collaboration without needing to speak.

choices.text: I need a short break from the noise. I will check back in when I am ready.
choices.feedback: Taking a break is a valid boundary. You can say what you plan to do without apologizing.

choices.text: I want to keep working, but I am not sure what would help yet.
choices.feedback: You do not have to know the perfect solution. You could try a quieter spot first, or take time to work out what you need.

cards: This space is too loud for me.
takeaway: Your sensory and communication needs are valid.

title: Setting boundaries
description: Protect your privacy and practice holding a boundary.
introduction: A boundary tells someone what you will or won’t do. You do not owe anyone your password. If someone keeps asking, you can repeat your boundary, leave, or ask a trusted person for support. Their behavior is not your fault.
scenario: A classmate, Alex, cannot open the class notes and asks to use your school account. You do not want anyone else using your login. Alex says it would only take a minute and that friends should trust each other. You can keep your account private, offer another way to share the notes if you want, or leave the conversation. Never enter a real password in this practice.
opening: Could I use your account to check the class notes?
question: What could you say or do to protect your privacy?

choices.text: I do not share access to my account.
choices.feedback: This is a clear boundary. You do not owe an apology or a longer explanation.

choices.text: I can send you a copy of the notes, but I am not sharing my login.
choices.feedback: This keeps your boundary and offers an alternative. Offering help is optional.

choices.text: I have said no. If you keep asking, I am going to leave.
choices.feedback: You can repeat a boundary and decide when to disengage. You are not responsible for making someone else respect it.

choices.text: End the conversation and ask a trusted person for support.
choices.feedback: You can leave or get support without continuing to explain. Someone else’s pressure is not your fault.

cards: I’ve said no. Please stop asking.
takeaway: You can say no and leave. You are not responsible for someone else’s pressure.

title: Misunderstandings
description: Clarify your meaning while making space for differences.
introduction: People can understand the same words differently. Misunderstandings can be mutual. You can explain what you meant, ask a question, disagree, or decide to stop.
scenario: You and Jordan are choosing an idea for a group project. Jordan suggests making a video. You ask “Why did you choose that?” because you want to understand the plan, but Jordan hears it as criticism and says you never like their ideas. You want to clarify what you meant and decide together whether to keep discussing the project.
opening: When you asked why I chose that idea, I thought you didn’t like it. Is that what you meant?
question: What could you say to clarify the misunderstanding or choose what happens next?

choices.text: I was asking how the video would work, not saying I disliked the idea.
choices.feedback: This explains your intention directly. Direct wording is a valid way to clear up a misunderstanding.

choices.text: What did you understand me to mean when I asked that?
choices.feedback: Asking about Jordan’s interpretation can help both of you see where the misunderstanding happened.

choices.text: I am unsure about making a video. Could we compare it with a written presentation?
choices.feedback: You can clarify your question and also disagree. You do not have to pretend to like the same idea.

choices.text: I would like to pause this conversation and talk about it later.
choices.feedback: You can ask to pause. Understanding each other is a shared responsibility, and you do not have to resolve everything immediately.

cards: Could you explain what you understood?
Can we talk about this later?
takeaway: Understanding each other is a shared responsibility.
